questions.question: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives. After several weeks, developers say the automated reviewer is noisy. Examples show comments about variable names, preferred assertion styles, and missing tests mixed with a few real null dereferences and authorization bypasses. The current prompt says, "Report only issues you are highly confident about." What prompt change would most directly improve review usefulness?

choices.text: Expand the checklist to include naming, formatting, test coverage, and architecture preferences so comments feel more comprehensive.
Define testable report and skip rules that focus comments on production bugs, security flaws, broken edge cases, and subtle regressions.
Keep the broad review scope and require each inline comment to include a numerical confidence score and short rationale.
Move every automated finding into a single nonblocking summary comment so developers can scan the noise separately.

explanations.A: This increases the very categories that are undermining developer trust. A broader checklist can make the review feel busy, but it moves attention away from correctness and security findings that developers need to act on.
explanations.B: This directly addresses the category boundary causing the noise. It tells the reviewer which findings are worth surfacing and which findings to skip, rather than asking it to estimate confidence on subjective issues.
explanations.C: Confidence scores do not decide whether an issue category is appropriate to report. The reviewer may be highly confident about a style preference, so this can preserve the same false positives in a more formal format.
explanations.D: Changing where findings appear does not fix whether they should be reported. Claude Code Code Review findings do not approve or block pull requests by default, so the main issue remains noisy selection criteria.

questions.questionExplanation: The failure mode is not that the reviewer lacks confidence metadata, it is that the prompt has not drawn a clear boundary between actionable correctness findings and low-value preference comments. "High confidence" is still subjective: a model can be confident that a variable name differs from a local style, even when that comment is not useful for a pull request review. Claude Code Code Review is documented as analyzing GitHub pull requests and posting severity-tagged inline findings for issues such as logic errors, security vulnerabilities, broken edge cases, and subtle regressions. The documentation also notes that its default calibration is for correctness, namely bugs that would break production, not formatting preferences or missing test coverage. See Claude Code Code Review. For CI review prompts, make the decision boundary concrete: report issues when the claimed or implemented behavior can break production, create a security risk, mishandle an edge case, or introduce a regression. Skip comments that are only style, naming, formatting, or local preference unless the team has explicitly made them part of the review objective. This reduces false positives and helps developers keep trusting the comments that matter.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. A customer support engineering team is building a resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK with MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). During testing, the agent trace shows Claude requesting lookup_order through MCP, but no order lookup result is observed and the session ends without a final customer response. What implementation change should this team make?

choices.text: Run all support MCP tools before starting the agent, then provide their outputs for Claude to summarize in one turn.
Parse the assistant's natural-language text for completion phrases, then end the workflow when it says the issue is resolved.
Add a system instruction that tells Claude to execute each MCP backend operation itself before producing any customer-facing response.
Run the SDK-driven agent loop so each MCP tool invocation is dispatched, results are returned, and processing continues until a final response.

explanations.A: Pre-running every tool removes Claude's ability to decide which actions are needed based on the case. It also risks unnecessary backend calls and does not support adaptive tool chaining across observations.
explanations.B: Natural-language text is not the reliable control signal for a tool loop. The implementation should rely on structured tool invocations and final-response signals rather than phrases in the assistant's response.
explanations.C: Prompt instructions can guide when Claude should request a tool, but they cannot make the model run backend code. MCP tool execution happens through the connected tool runtime, not inside the model itself.
explanations.D: Claude can request tool use, but the model does not execute backend operations by itself. The agent runtime or surrounding application must keep processing tool invocations and returned observations until Claude produces a final response.

questions.questionExplanation: Tool use is a contract between Claude and the surrounding runtime. In an Agent SDK system with MCP tools, Claude can decide that it needs a tool and emit a structured tool invocation, but the model itself does not perform backend operations such as customer or order lookups. The practical requirement is that the agent runtime or application must keep the agentic loop alive: dispatch requested MCP tool calls to the connected tool server or runtime, return the results as observations, and let Claude continue reasoning from those observations until it produces a final customer-facing response. If the host process stops after the tool request, the transcript will show a valid request but no completed action or final answer. This design lets Claude choose actions adaptively while preserving a clear execution boundary around external systems. Prompt-only fixes and text parsing confuse guidance with control, while pre-running every tool turns an adaptive agent into a fixed workflow with unnecessary calls. See Anthropic's How tool use works documentation for the underlying tool-use contract and execution responsibilities.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. A customer support resolution agent's production logs show that process_refund sometimes returns a successful-looking tool result with content "Refund blocked by policy" when an order is outside the refund window. Claude then retries the same refund call with slightly different wording instead of explaining the policy outcome or escalating when appropriate. What change would best improve the agent's recovery behavior?

choices.text: Update the process_refund description to warn Claude not to request refunds outside the configured refund window.
Return a normal CallToolResult with a longer refund policy explanation and suggested next steps in the content blocks.
Raise a JSON-RPC protocol error from tools/call whenever the refund request violates a configured business policy.
Return a CallToolResult with isError: true and place custom errorCategory, isRetryable, and policy text in structuredContent.

explanations.A: Improving the description can reduce some bad tool selection, but it does not solve recovery after the backend detects a policy violation. The agent still needs a structured signal from the tool result when the request is validly formed but cannot be completed.
explanations.B: A longer message may be clearer to a human, but it still presents the policy block as a normal successful result. Without isError: true and structured recovery metadata, the agent has a weaker signal for deciding whether to retry, explain, or escalate.
explanations.C: JSON-RPC errors are best reserved for protocol-level failures such as malformed requests or unavailable methods, not expected domain outcomes from a valid tool invocation. A policy denial is a tool execution result that the model needs to reason about, so it should be returned as a tool result with explicit error semantics.
explanations.D: This uses the official MCP error indicator to tell the agent the tool execution did not complete successfully. The category, retryability hint, and user-facing policy message are custom metadata, so they belong in structuredContent or another agreed output schema rather than being treated as standard MCP fields.

questions.questionExplanation: For customer support tools, the important distinction is between a successful business outcome, a retryable operational failure, and a non-retryable policy denial. If a backend returns a policy denial as ordinary text in a successful-looking result, Claude may interpret the result as ambiguous and try again. Marking the tool result with isError: true gives the agent the documented MCP signal that the tool execution failed, while custom metadata such as errorCategory and isRetryable can provide the recovery policy your application wants. MCP tool calls are made through the tools/call method with a tool name and optional arguments. A CallToolResult returns content blocks and can also include structured content when the tool provides machine-readable output. Fields such as errorCategory and isRetryable are useful design conventions, but they are not the standard MCP error marker, so they should be treated as custom structured output. The design tradeoff is that structured errors require more implementation discipline, but they make agent behavior more predictable under failure. In a refund workflow, this helps prevent wasteful retry loops and supports safer resolution behavior. See the MCP tool and schema documentation at MCP Tools and MCP Schema.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. Your team created a Claude Code skill called `literature-gap-audit`. Its `SKILL.md` tells Claude to search repository prompts, inspect report templates, and brainstorm missing provenance checks before anyone edits the coordinator. When developers invoke it, pages of file-search notes and rejected alternatives remain in the main session, and later report-generation edits become less focused. What should you change in the skill configuration?

choices.text: Invoke `/fork` for the audit so it inherits the full current conversation history.
Move the audit instructions into `CLAUDE.md` and run `/compact` after the audit finishes.
Set `disable-model-invocation: true` and leave the audit in the main conversation.
Add `context: fork` in `SKILL.md` and keep the audit as explicit task instructions.

explanations.A: `/fork` is a separate Claude Code mechanism that can isolate a side task while inheriting the current conversation. It does not modify `SKILL.md` frontmatter or make this skill run as a forked skill when invoked, so it is not the requested skill configuration change.
explanations.B: `CLAUDE.md` is loaded as persistent project context, so putting a verbose occasional workflow there makes every session carry more guidance than it needs. `/compact` can reduce context after the fact, but it does not prevent exploratory output from entering the main session.
explanations.C: Disabling model invocation controls whether Claude can automatically invoke the skill, which is useful for workflows that should be triggered manually. It does not run the skill in an isolated context or prevent verbose intermediate work from filling the main session.
explanations.D: This runs the skill in a forked subagent context, so verbose discovery work happens outside the main conversation and only the useful result returns. It is appropriate because the skill contains an actionable audit workflow, not just passive reference guidance.

questions.questionExplanation: Use context: fork when a Claude Code skill performs a side task that would otherwise flood the main conversation with search results, logs, file contents, or exploratory alternatives. In a forked skill, the rendered SKILL.md content drives work in a separate subagent context, and the main session receives the useful result rather than the full discovery trail. This pattern fits task and workflow skills with explicit instructions, such as an audit that searches prompts and report templates before recommending provenance improvements. It is not a good fit for passive reference material, such as API conventions, because the subagent would receive guidelines without a concrete task to perform. CLAUDE.md, /compact, and disable-model-invocation solve different problems. CLAUDE.md is persistent context, /compact compresses an already noisy conversation, and disable-model-invocation controls automatic skill invocation. Also avoid confusing skill frontmatter context: fork with /fork: /fork can isolate a side task while inheriting the full conversation, but it is not a SKILL.md configuration setting. Learn more in the official Claude Code slash commands and skills documentation, the Subagents documentation, and the Claude Code context documentation.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. A payments platform team is about to migrate a shared logging library used across more than 45 files. Two viable integration approaches have different infrastructure requirements, and the maintainers want Claude Code to inspect the codebase and propose an approach before implementation begins. Which initial workflow is most appropriate?

choices.text: Start in acceptEdits, let Claude apply the migration, and review the resulting diff after the changes finish.
Start in bypassPermissions, let Claude run commands freely, and rely on tests to identify any regressions afterward.
Enter plan mode, have Claude inspect the affected areas, and review the proposed plan before choosing execution mode.
Start with a direct implementation prompt, ask Claude to choose an approach, and refine the design during editing.

explanations.A: acceptEdits is oriented toward approving edits automatically, which skips the planning checkpoint the maintainers need. Reviewing a completed diff is useful, but it happens after Claude has already made broad changes across the codebase.
explanations.B: bypassPermissions is not an appropriate default for creating an architectural plan because it allows broad tool use rather than preserving a review gate. Tests are valuable during implementation, but they do not replace selecting an approach before files are changed.
explanations.C: Plan mode is designed to separate exploration and planning from implementation. It fits a large, uncertain migration because Claude can investigate the codebase and present a plan without editing source files until the plan is approved.
explanations.D: A direct implementation prompt blends design exploration with code changes. That is better suited to small, well-scoped tasks, not a migration with multiple valid approaches and infrastructure tradeoffs.

questions.questionExplanation: Plan mode in Claude Code is a permission mode for analysis before implementation, not a different model or subscription tier. It lets Claude inspect the codebase and develop a plan while avoiding source file edits until the user approves the plan, which is exactly the control point needed for large migrations and architecture-sensitive changes. Anthropic's best-practices guidance recommends planning when the approach is uncertain, when many files may change, or when the developer needs exploration before committing to an implementation path. After Claude presents a plan, approving it exits plan mode and switches into a selected execution mode, such as reviewing each edit manually or accepting edits. For a typo, log line, or simple rename, this checkpoint can be unnecessary, but for a 45-plus-file migration with infrastructure implications, separating planning from editing reduces avoidable churn and makes the architectural decision explicit. See Claude Code permission modes and Claude Code best practices for the documented behavior and recommended use cases.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. In this team's monorepo, unit and component tests sit next to the source files they cover under services/, packages/, and apps/. Claude Code applies inconsistent testing guidance because similar instructions were copied into several directory-level memory files, and some directories are missing updates. What should you change to make the testing convention easier to maintain while avoiding unnecessary context for non-test work?

choices.text: Add a `CLAUDE.md` file to every directory that contains tests and duplicate the shared testing conventions there.
Create a `.claude/rules/testing.md` file with `paths` globs for test files and store the shared testing conventions there.
Move the testing conventions into the root `CLAUDE.md` so Claude loads them during all project conversations.
Put the testing conventions in a project slash command under `.claude/commands/` and ask developers to run it before editing tests.

questions.questionExplanation: The memory docs prescribe `.claude/rules/` with `paths` frontmatter for exactly this pattern: rules "can also be scoped to specific file paths, so they only load into context when Claude works with matching files," and each file "should cover one topic, with a descriptive filename like `testing.md`." One `.claude/rules/testing.md` with test-file globs gives a single source of truth that stays consistent across `services/`, `packages/`, and `apps/`, and it stays out of context during non-test work. A is wrong because per-directory duplication is what caused the inconsistency and missing updates in the first place. C is wrong because the root CLAUDE.md loads unconditionally in every session, adding testing context to non-test work and pushing the file past the recommended 200-line target. D is wrong because a slash command must be invoked manually by developers, so the convention applies only when someone remembers to run it. Reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. This team’s custom /upgrade-plan command parses repository upgrade guides into JSON for downstream automation. Evals show valid JSON, but required fields such as rollback_command and compatibility_note are returned as null when the source expresses them in fenced shell blocks, Markdown checklists, or prose paragraphs. The information is present in the source, and the current prompt already lists the schema and says not to omit required fields. What change would most directly address the extraction failures?

choices.text: Move the schema description into CLAUDE.md so it is always loaded for the command.
Raise the temperature to encourage broader interpretation of each upgrade guide format.
Add 3 to 5 structured examples that map varied guide formats to the expected JSON fields.
Add a stronger instruction that required JSON fields must never be null or empty.

explanations.A: Putting general instructions in CLAUDE.md can help shared project context, but it does not address the specific extraction ambiguity. The prompt already describes the schema, so the missing ingredient is demonstrated handling of representative formats.
explanations.B: Higher temperature increases output variability, which is usually counterproductive for extraction tasks that need consistency. The issue is not a lack of creativity, it is an unclear decision boundary for recognizing required fields across formats.
explanations.C: Few-shot or multishot examples are well suited when a model must learn how different input patterns correspond to the same output fields. Relevant, diverse, structured examples can demonstrate that fenced commands, checklist items, and prose notes all count as valid evidence for the required fields.
explanations.D: A stronger instruction may increase pressure to fill fields, but it does not teach how to identify the values in varied document structures. It can also encourage fabrication when a field is genuinely absent, so it is weaker than showing grounded examples.

questions.questionExplanation: When extraction fails even though the source contains the information, the prompt often needs to teach Claude the mapping behavior, not merely repeat the target schema. Few-shot or multishot prompting is designed for this kind of consistency problem: the examples show that a rollback command in a fenced shell block, a checklist item, or a prose sentence can all populate the same JSON field. Anthropic recommends making examples relevant, diverse, and structured, with examples wrapped in <example> tags and multiple examples grouped inside <examples>. For this command, the best examples would mirror real upgrade guides and include both the source excerpt and the ideal extracted JSON, so Claude learns the decision boundary without being pushed to invent values. See Use examples (multishot prompting) to guide Claude's behavior.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. This team wants to move non-urgent post-resolution quality checks to the Message Batches API. Cases arrive continuously, and each check must reach a terminal batch outcome within 30 hours of case arrival for audit triage. Assume a batch may take the full documented 24-hour processing window before results are available or the batch expires. Which submission cadence should the team use?

choices.text: Submit accumulated requests every 12 hours, using custom_id to correlate each case outcome.
Submit accumulated requests once daily, using custom_id to correlate each case outcome.
Submit accumulated requests every 8 hours, using custom_id to correlate each case outcome.
Submit accumulated requests every 4 hours, using custom_id to correlate each case outcome.

explanations.A: A 12-hour accumulation window can create a worst-case timeline of 36 hours before the batch reaches a terminal outcome. This cadence is too slow for the stated SLA even though it may reduce operational overhead.
explanations.B: A daily submission cadence can make a newly arrived case wait close to 24 hours before it is submitted. Adding the possible 24-hour batch window makes this incompatible with a 30-hour SLA.
explanations.C: An 8-hour accumulation window can create a worst-case timeline of 32 hours before the team knows the terminal outcome. That exceeds the stated 30-hour SLA when batch processing takes the full documented window.
explanations.D: A 30-hour business SLA with a possible 24-hour batch processing window leaves at most 6 hours for pre-submission accumulation. Submitting every 4 hours keeps the worst-case timeline within the SLA and leaves a 2-hour buffer.

questions.questionExplanation: The useful mental model for the Message Batches API is that it is an asynchronous processing mechanism for large volumes of Messages API requests, not a low-latency path for urgent work. For SLA planning, separate the time an item waits before submission from the time Anthropic may spend processing the batch. Here the SLA is 30 hours from item arrival, and the assumed batch-processing window is 24 hours. That leaves 30 - 24 = 6 hours as the maximum safe accumulation window before submission. A 4-hour cadence fits within that bound and leaves 2 hours of buffer, while 8 hours, 12 hours, and daily submission can exceed the SLA in the worst case. The 24-hour point should be treated carefully: the documentation describes when results become accessible or when a batch may expire, not a guarantee that every request succeeds within 24 hours. Each request should still use a valid, unique custom_id so downstream systems can correlate outcomes back to the originating support case. See Anthropic's Message Batches API documentation for the asynchronous processing model, batch limits, result availability behavior, and custom_id guidance.

questions.question: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives. Long pull requests are causing the review step to run near the context limit. The trace shows each file-analysis tool call appends a large tool_result payload with build metadata, ownership data, full lint output, historical CI runs, and dependency details, even though the reviewer uses only a small subset of those fields. What change best addresses the reliability issue?

choices.text: Apply prompt caching to the tool definitions and repeated review prefix to reduce context-window pressure.
Change the tool wrapper to return compact, review-specific tool_result payloads with only the fields needed.
Increase max_tokens for the review response and instruct Claude to ignore irrelevant tool-result fields.
Enable context editing to clear old tool results after the request crosses a configured threshold.

explanations.A: Prompt caching can reduce cost and latency for repeated prefixes, but it does not reduce the number of tokens counted in the context window. It is useful for repeated static content, not for removing oversized dynamic tool results from the model's working context.
explanations.B: This directly reduces the amount of tool output added to the conversation history. Since tool_result blocks count toward the context window, shaping results before they enter context preserves room for the review evidence that actually matters.
explanations.C: The max_tokens setting controls how much Claude may generate, not how much input context is available for accumulated tool results. Asking Claude to ignore irrelevant fields does not prevent those fields from consuming context before the model can ignore them.
explanations.D: Context editing can remove older tool_result blocks before the prompt reaches Claude, which can help with stale accumulated history. It does not address the immediate root cause that each fresh file-analysis result is much larger than the review needs.

questions.questionExplanation: Tool-heavy review agents often fail because tool results become part of the conversation context. Anthropic documents that tool definitions and accumulated tool_result blocks can exhaust context in long-running agents, and the context window includes messages, tool results, tool definitions, and generated output. See Manage tool context and Context windows. The right mental model is that every field returned by a tool is something Claude must carry forward if it remains in messages. A 40-field payload is not harmless just because the prompt says only a few fields matter. The most reliable fix is to shape the tool output before creating the tool_result, returning only the review-relevant evidence needed for the next reasoning step. Other mechanisms solve different problems. Prompt caching can reduce billing and latency for repeated prefixes, but cached tokens still count toward the context window. Context editing can clear older tool results, but it is not a substitute for designing compact current tool outputs. The tool lifecycle itself is documented in Handle tool calls, where tool results are returned inside normal user messages rather than a separate tool role.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. During a billing dispute flow, Claude requests get_customer and lookup_order in the same assistant turn. The get_customer call succeeds, but lookup_order intermittently times out. Production logs show two attempted fixes: one wrapper returns an empty order list as a successful lookup, while another aborts the entire conversation whenever lookup_order fails. What change best addresses the reliability issue?

choices.text: Return tool results for both calls, replace lookup_order with an empty order list, and continue as a successful lookup.
Return tool results for both calls, flag lookup_order with is_error: true, and continue from partial context.
Return tool results for both calls, discard get_customer after lookup_order fails, and end the support workflow.
Return tool results for completed calls only, omit lookup_order after its timeout, and ask Claude to proceed.

explanations.A: This hides the difference between a real no-order result and a tool execution failure. It can cause the agent to make incorrect customer-support decisions because the coordinator receives false evidence rather than an actionable error.
explanations.B: This preserves the required tool-result protocol while giving Claude accurate information about the failed operation. The agent can use the successful customer data, reason about retrying or escalating, and avoid incorrectly treating a timeout as proof that no orders exist.
explanations.C: This avoids silent data loss, but it is too brittle for workflows where partial results may still support recovery or escalation. A single transient lookup failure should not automatically discard successful tool results or prevent the agent from making a reasoned next step.
explanations.D: This violates the expected tool-use exchange because every tool_use block needs a corresponding tool_result. It also deprives Claude of explicit error context, and malformed tool-result ordering or missing results can cause request-level errors.

questions.questionExplanation: Tool failures should be treated as part of the agent's observed state, not hidden or converted into misleading business facts. When Claude emits tool_use, the application is expected to execute the requested client tools and return matching tool_result blocks, using the same tool_use_id so Claude can connect each result to the right call. The reliable pattern is to return all available results and mark failed executions with is_error: true. This lets the agent distinguish three materially different situations: the customer has no orders, the order service failed, or the order service returned partial information. Those distinctions matter in support workflows because they drive different next actions, such as retrying, asking a clarifying question, or escalating to a human. Silently returning an empty success is an anti-pattern because it changes an operational failure into false domain evidence. Terminating the whole workflow on one failure is also an anti-pattern because it throws away useful context from successful calls and prevents graceful degradation. The tool-use protocol is designed so the model can continue reasoning from accurate observations, while actual API request failures remain separate from successful Messages API responses and their stop_reason control flow. See Anthropic's guidance on Handle tool calls for tool-result formatting and is_error, and Handling stop reasons for how successful responses require control-flow decisions rather than a single success or failure branch.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. The team is refactoring long cases into a coordinator that can delegate billing and returns investigation steps. During testing, a container crash mid-dispute causes the replacement worker to lose the verified customer ID, prior order findings, and a decision that the case must be escalated. The workers do not share a filesystem, and local session JSONL files are not reliably present after restart. What change best supports safe crash recovery?

choices.text: Resume the Agent SDK session with continue, then let the coordinator reconstruct state from the latest local transcript.
Add stronger memory instructions to the system prompt, then restart the agent from the last customer message.
Persist an application-defined JSON state manifest, then load it on restart and inject it into coordinator and subagent prompts.
Copy local JSONL transcript files opportunistically, then resume whichever session appears newest on the replacement worker.

explanations.A: The continue behavior finds the most recent session in the current directory, which is unsafe when the intended prior run must be selected precisely. This also depends on local session files being present at the expected path, which the situation says is not reliable.
explanations.B: Stronger prompt instructions do not create durable memory across crashes or independent API calls. Restarting from the last customer message omits tool results and decisions that are needed to avoid unsafe duplicate or inconsistent actions.
explanations.C: This treats crash recovery facts as durable application state rather than assuming the next worker can access a local session file. Loading the JSON state manifest and injecting it into coordinator and subagent prompts makes the verified IDs, prior findings, and escalation decision explicit after restart.
explanations.D: Restoring a transcript can be valid only when the JSONL file is restored to the expected path and working directory, or when a documented session store is used. Opportunistically copying files and choosing the newest session risks resuming the wrong case or failing on a replacement host.

questions.questionExplanation: For crash recovery, distinguish conversation transcript from application state. Agent SDK sessions record the prompt, tool calls, tool results, and responses, but they are stored locally by path and host, so autoscaled workers that do not share a filesystem cannot rely on local JSONL availability. The safer pattern here is an application-defined state manifest, optionally produced with outputFormat or output_format using type: "json_schema", that captures the verified customer, relevant order facts, actions already taken, pending escalation, and decisions the coordinator must honor. On recovery, the coordinator should load that durable manifest and include it explicitly in its own prompt and in any subagent delegation prompts. This avoids the common failure mode where a new agent has a transcript fragment or last user message but not the business-critical facts needed to avoid duplicate refunds or missed escalations. If the team does need transcript continuity across hosts, use documented mechanisms such as restoring the JSONL transcript to the same path and CWD or a SessionStore, while remembering that SessionStore mirrors transcripts and has best-effort write behavior rather than replacing durable application state. See Agent SDK Sessions, Session Storage, and Structured Outputs.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. Production traces show that every incoming request is sent through separate identity, order, refund-policy, and escalation-summary subagents. Simple order-status questions now have high latency, and some responses include irrelevant refund-policy caveats. What change best improves the design while preserving specialized workers for cases that need them?

choices.text: Route every case through all subagents, then ask the final responder to remove irrelevant findings before answering.
Replace the subagents with one large system prompt that covers identity, orders, refunds, and escalation.
Add a coordinator step that inspects the case, invokes only needed subagents, and passes each a self-contained task summary.
Give every subagent the same backend tools, then instruct each worker to skip itself when it is not needed.

explanations.A: This preserves the root cause: every request still pays the latency and context cost of the full pipeline. A cleanup prompt can reduce visible noise, but it does not prevent unnecessary subagent execution or irrelevant intermediate analysis.
explanations.B: This removes the isolation and specialization benefits that subagents provide for self-contained investigations. A monolithic prompt can also increase attention dilution when only a small part of the capability set is relevant.
explanations.C: This design keeps the benefits of specialized subagents while avoiding unnecessary work on simple cases. Because subagents have isolated context, the coordinator must explicitly provide the relevant case facts and task scope to each worker it invokes.
explanations.D: This delegates routing responsibility to every worker instead of centralizing it in the coordinator. It also broadens tool access unnecessarily, which increases blast radius compared with per-worker tool restrictions.

questions.questionExplanation: A good coordinator does not treat every request as if it needs the maximum workflow. It should analyze the current case, determine which capabilities are actually needed, and delegate only the self-contained pieces of work that benefit from a specialized worker. Subagents are useful because they run in their own context window with their own instructions and tool access, then return results to the caller. That isolation is valuable for verbose investigations, but it also means the coordinator must pass the necessary facts explicitly rather than assuming the worker shares the main conversation context. The common anti-pattern is an always full pipeline: identity, order, refund, and escalation analysis all run even when the customer only needs a simple answer. This wastes latency and can introduce irrelevant caveats into the final response. A coordinator-level routing step preserves specialization while reducing unnecessary work and limiting tool exposure. Anthropic documents description-driven delegation, isolated subagent context, and tool restrictions for subagents in Claude Code sub-agents. For API-based tool orchestration, Claude can also decide on each turn whether to call tools under automatic tool choice, as described in Tool use overview.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. Benchmark runs on broad topics are slow and produce uneven coverage. Logs show the coordinator asks one specialist to research every dimension, passes a compressed prose summary to the next specialist, and only then asks for the final report. The relevant dimensions are known at the start and do not depend on one another. What design change best improves latency and coverage while preserving a coherent final report?

choices.text: Have each specialist hand off unfinished dimensions to another specialist, merge their private context, and return a consolidated answer to the coordinator.
Have the coordinator split the request into dimension-specific subtasks, pass shared constraints to each, invoke independent specialists together, and synthesize their findings.
Have the coordinator disable parallel tool use, process each dimension in separate turns, append every raw result, and synthesize after the last subtask.
Have the coordinator keep one broad subtask, increase the search specialist's source budget, pass its summary downstream, and request a completeness critique.

explanations.A: This weakens the coordinator's orchestration role and creates unclear ownership of coverage and provenance. Subagents do not automatically share private context, so relying on peer handoffs can lose important assumptions and source mappings.
explanations.B: This uses parallel decomposition for independent workstreams while keeping a single coordinator responsible for final synthesis. Passing shared constraints to each specialist preserves the common context needed for consistent scope, citation expectations, and report structure.
explanations.C: Sequential processing can improve separation of concerns, but it gives up the latency benefit available when dimensions are independent. Appending every raw result also risks bloating context rather than passing high-signal, structured findings forward.
explanations.D: Increasing source volume does not address the decomposition problem that causes uneven attention across dimensions. A completeness critique can catch some gaps, but it happens after upstream work has already compressed or omitted important findings.

questions.questionExplanation: For independent research dimensions, the strongest pattern is to split, run, collect, then synthesize. The coordinator should create distinct subtasks, provide each specialist with the shared scope, constraints, and citation requirements, then combine their structured findings into one coherent report. Claude can emit several tool_use blocks in a single assistant turn, and the application decides whether those client-side calls run concurrently, sequentially, or with a mixed strategy. The official guidance on parallel tool use notes that independent, read-only calls are usually good candidates for parallel execution, while work with side effects or ordering dependencies should be handled more carefully. The practical boundary is that parallelism is not a substitute for context design. Each specialist needs the shared instructions and enough source or metadata context to do its work, and the coordinator should collect one tool_result for each tool_use before moving to synthesis. The result formatting requirements are described in handle tool calls, including matching tool_use_id values and returning the results in the next user message. The tradeoff is fan-out cost and complexity. The orchestration guidance in mid-conversation effort example describes this pattern as useful for separable subtasks, but it also cautions that spawning many workstreams can multiply token usage. Use it when the subtasks are genuinely independent and the final synthesis benefits from broader, more balanced coverage.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. The team keeps refund and escalation policy changes in GitHub and requests managed Claude Code Review only during scheduled review batches. A reviewer comments `@claude review once`, fixes are pushed, and then a second `@claude review once` repeats several resolved findings as new inline comments. They want the next manual re-review to preserve reviewer trust while still surfacing any unresolved issue from the first review. What should they change?

choices.text: Add `REVIEW.md` guidance that uses prior findings during re-reviews and reports only new or still-unresolved issues.
Keep review instructions unchanged and have maintainers close any duplicate inline threads after each re-review.
Change the manual command to `@claude review` so the PR subscribes to push-triggered reviews for the remaining work.
Rerun the review from the GitHub Checks tab so Claude Code refreshes comments against the new commit.

explanations.A: `REVIEW.md` is the documented configuration point for review-only guidance in Claude Code Review. This directly addresses duplicate comments by shaping the review behavior rather than relying on trigger mechanics or manual cleanup.
explanations.B: Manual cleanup treats the symptom after duplicate comments have already appeared. It does not improve the review agent's behavior, and repeated duplicate findings can reduce developer trust in legitimate review feedback.
explanations.C: `@claude review` starts a review and subscribes the PR to future push-triggered reviews, while `@claude review once` performs a single review. Changing the trigger mode does not by itself tell Claude how to handle prior findings or avoid repeating resolved comments.
explanations.D: The GitHub Checks Re-run button is not the documented way to retrigger managed Claude Code Review. The documented options are to comment with the review command or push a new commit when the PR is already subscribed to push-triggered reviews.

questions.questionExplanation: Repeated review runs need more than access to the current diff. The review should be given a clear comparison task: consider the prior findings, then report only issues that are new or still unaddressed. In managed Claude Code Review, the documented place for review-specific guidance is REVIEW.md, which is injected into the review pipeline as review guidance. The trigger mechanism and the review behavior are separate concerns. @claude review once starts a single manual review, while @claude review starts a review and subscribes the PR to future push-triggered reviews. Switching commands can change when reviews happen, but it does not define how to deduplicate findings across re-runs. Also avoid relying on the GitHub Checks Re-run button for this feature, since the documentation states that it does not retrigger managed Code Review. The practical pattern is to configure the review instructions so re-runs preserve signal quality, then invoke reviews using the documented command flow. See Claude Code Review.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. During evaluation, final reports cite sources but sometimes treat a peer-reviewed study, a vendor benchmark, and an internal survey as equivalent evidence for the same claim. The search and document-analysis subagents currently return concise finding summaries plus a general list of sources consulted. What change best supports accurate downstream synthesis?

choices.text: Add a report-generation pass that expands the final narrative with a separate bibliography and citation appendix.
Give each subagent broader tool access so it can inspect all available sources before summarizing its findings.
Ask the coordinator to retain full subagent transcripts and have the synthesizer infer provenance from prior work.
Require each subagent to return structured claim records with source location, publication date, evidence excerpt, and methodology notes.

explanations.A: A bibliography helps readers find sources, but it does not reliably connect each claim to the exact evidence and methodological context behind it. Once the synthesis step has already merged unlike evidence, a later formatting pass cannot reconstruct missing provenance.
explanations.B: Broader tool access may increase coverage, but it does not require the subagent to return the metadata needed for synthesis. It can also add more context and tool output without solving the provenance loss in the handoff.
explanations.C: This assumes downstream agents can reliably recover details that were not included in the returned handoff. Non-fork subagents work in isolated contexts, and relying on inference from bulky transcripts is less reliable than requiring structured claim metadata.
explanations.D: This makes provenance and methodological context part of the handoff contract rather than something the synthesizer must reconstruct later. Because subagents return only what they provide back to the main conversation, the coordinator needs these fields preserved in the returned summary.

questions.questionExplanation: In a multi-agent research system, provenance is an interface contract. A subagent may perform a rich investigation, but downstream agents can only depend on the information that is explicitly returned in its summary or handoff. If the returned output says only that a source supports a finding, the synthesizer may lose the distinction between evidence types, time periods, source locations, and methods. Claude Code subagents are designed for context management: they handle work in their own context and return a summary to the main conversation. The official subagents documentation notes that non-fork subagents start with a fresh, isolated context and do not automatically share the parent conversation history, which makes explicit handoff content essential. See Claude Code subagents. The reliable pattern is to require structured claim records, for example: claim, evidence excerpt, source URL or document location, publication or collection date, and methodology notes. This is not just a citation formatting preference; it prevents the synthesis agent from treating incomparable evidence as interchangeable. Anthropic's tool-use guidance also emphasizes returning high-signal fields rather than bloated responses, which supports concise but complete provenance handoffs. See Implement tool use.

questions.question: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives. After three months, the system described above assigns a high confidence score to most structured review findings and generated test recommendations. Manual review capacity is being reduced, but the team still needs to measure production error rates and catch rare failure modes in areas like migrations, security-sensitive changes, and language-specific conventions. What monitoring approach best fits this goal?

choices.text: Sample high-confidence findings within strata for change type, component, language, and finding category, then label errors and novel patterns separately.
Increase the confidence cutoff for findings before merging, then discontinue review for outputs above the new cutoff.
Sample high-confidence findings uniformly across all repositories, then publish one aggregate error rate for the whole pipeline.
Sample only low-confidence findings within queues for human review, then treat high-confidence accepted pull requests as error-free cases.

explanations.A: This preserves visibility into high-confidence outputs while focusing limited reviewer capacity on meaningful segments of the production distribution. Stratifying by factors that affect review quality helps reveal pockets of poor performance that a single overall metric could hide.
explanations.B: Raising a threshold may reduce the number of outputs labeled high confidence, but it does not validate whether the remaining high-confidence outputs are correct. Discontinuing review removes the feedback loop needed to detect drift and new error patterns.
explanations.C: Uniform random sampling can estimate a broad error rate, but it may miss rare but important segments such as security-sensitive changes or migration code. Reporting only one aggregate metric can mask failures concentrated in specific languages, components, or finding categories.
explanations.D: Low-confidence review is useful for routing obvious risk to humans, but it does not measure whether high-confidence outputs are actually reliable. Treating accepted pull requests as error-free can hide systematic false negatives and novel failure modes.

questions.questionExplanation: For a CI review system, high confidence should not mean no measurement. It should mean the output is eligible for lighter review, while a designed sample of those outputs is still checked so the team can estimate real error rates and detect unexpected failures. Stratified random sampling is the right pattern when errors may vary by segment. Sampling within strata such as change type, component, language, and finding category gives visibility into segments that might be rare overall but operationally important. This avoids the common trap of relying on aggregate accuracy, where a strong overall number can hide poor performance on a small but high-impact class of pull requests. Anthropic’s evaluation guidance emphasizes defining task-specific, measurable success criteria and designing evaluations that mirror real-world task distributions, including edge cases. That maps directly to ongoing production monitoring: choose strata that reflect meaningful differences in the CI workload, label sampled outputs, track per-stratum error rates, and record novel patterns so prompts, rubrics, or review routing can be improved. See Define success criteria.

questions.question: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives. During a PR review run, the main session reads the changed files, notes a failing test, and then delegates to an ordinary named security-review subagent, not a fork. The subagent returns generic findings and misses PR-specific evidence from the diff and test output. What change would most directly improve the review's reliability?

choices.text: Start a fresh named subagent invocation and rely on its persisted transcript from earlier CI steps.
Instruct the subagent to read the parent conversation transcript before producing review findings.
Compact the main conversation before delegation so the subagent inherits only the important parent context.
Include the changed files, key diff excerpts, failing test output, and review criteria in the subagent prompt.

explanations.A: Each new named subagent invocation starts with fresh context. Persisted subagent transcripts are separate from the main conversation, and continuing previous subagent work requires resuming that subagent rather than starting a new one.
explanations.B: An ordinary named subagent does not automatically see the parent conversation history. Asking it to use context it cannot access does not make the prior file reads or test results available.
explanations.C: Compaction can help manage the main conversation's context, but it does not cause a non-fork subagent to inherit that context. The subagent still receives task-specific parent context through the delegation message rather than through the compacted transcript.
explanations.D: This directly addresses how ordinary named subagents receive task-specific context. A non-fork subagent starts with its own context, so the delegation prompt must carry the PR facts it needs to perform a grounded review.

questions.questionExplanation: Ordinary named Claude Code subagents are designed for isolated, task-specific work. That isolation is valuable in CI because a security reviewer can have its own instructions, tool access, and permissions, while the main review conversation avoids being flooded with every intermediate step. The tradeoff is that the subagent does not automatically know what the main session already read or decided. For a non-fork subagent, the practical handoff pattern is to put the needed evidence directly in the delegation prompt: changed files, important diff excerpts, failing test output, relevant assumptions, and the review criteria. Without that explicit context, the subagent may fall back to generic review patterns, which increases false positives and misses PR-specific issues. A fork is the documented exception because it inherits the parent conversation, but the situation uses an ordinary named subagent. Compaction, CLAUDE.md guidance, and separate persisted transcripts can be useful for other context-management problems, but they do not replace a complete task message for a fresh non-fork subagent. Learn more in Claude Code subagents.

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. During evaluation, the synthesis subagent receives a long concatenation of subagent outputs. It repeatedly omits well-supported findings that appear midway through the bundle, while preserving findings near the start and end. What change would best reduce this failure while keeping the synthesis step grounded in the original evidence?

choices.text: Replace detailed evidence with progressively shorter summaries, then pass only the newest summary to the synthesis agent.
Move all source URLs to a final appendix, then keep the narrative evidence together in one continuous section.
Prepend a concise findings map before the aggregated outputs, then group detailed evidence under explicit source and topic headers.
Concatenate subagent outputs in completion order, then ask the synthesis agent to infer the main themes from the full bundle.

explanations.A: Repeated summarization can reduce token usage, but each pass risks losing nuance, qualifiers, and source-specific details. This is especially risky for research reports where claims must remain tied to evidence.
explanations.B: Separating sources from claims weakens claim-source mapping and makes verification harder during synthesis. A continuous narrative section also gives the model fewer structural cues for finding and comparing evidence.
explanations.C: This directly addresses position sensitivity by placing the most important synthesis cues where they are easier for the model to use. Explicit headers also make the detailed evidence easier to navigate without removing the provenance needed for cited reporting.
explanations.D: Completion order is convenient for orchestration logs, but it is not optimized for model attention or synthesis quality. Asking the model to infer the structure leaves important findings buried in a long middle section.

questions.questionExplanation: Long-context systems should not treat a large context window as a guarantee that every part of the input will receive equal attention. A practical mitigation is to put a key findings summary or findings map at the beginning of the aggregated input, then organize the supporting material with clear section boundaries so the synthesis agent can locate the relevant evidence. For a multi-agent research system, this pattern preserves both recall and provenance. The coordinator can present a front-loaded map of major claims, coverage gaps, conflicts, and source groupings, while the full subagent outputs remain available underneath explicit topic and source headers. This is different from compressing everything into a final summary, which can make the report less grounded and harder to cite. Anthropic guidance on long-context prompting emphasizes careful prompt organization and clear structure for large inputs. See Long context prompting tips for related guidance on making long inputs easier for Claude to use.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. A nightly pull request check for this team invokes Claude Code to inspect changes to refund and escalation logic. In CI, the job prints the prompt and then waits until the runner times out because there is no terminal user to answer follow-up prompts. What change best prevents this failure mode?

choices.text: Add a CLAUDE.md instruction telling Claude Code not to ask follow-up questions during CI reviews.
Run Claude Code in plan mode and require the job to approve the generated plan automatically.
Create a shared slash command in .claude/commands/ and invoke that command from the CI job.
Run Claude Code with the -p or --print flag and provide the review prompt non-interactively.

explanations.A: CLAUDE.md can provide project context and review criteria, but it is prompt guidance rather than the CI execution mode. It may reduce some clarifying questions, but it does not prevent the CLI process from running interactively.
explanations.B: Plan mode is useful when a developer needs to review an approach before implementation, especially for complex code changes. It does not by itself make Claude Code non-interactive, so it can still be a poor fit for unattended CI execution.
explanations.C: A project slash command can standardize the team's review checklist and prompt wording. It does not change the process into non-interactive mode, so the job still needs the appropriate CLI invocation for automation.
explanations.D: The -p or --print flag is designed for non-interactive Claude Code runs, such as CI jobs. It processes the supplied prompt, writes the result, and exits instead of waiting for additional terminal input.

questions.questionExplanation: Claude Code has an interactive terminal mode for developer sessions and a non-interactive mode for automation. In CI, there is no human sitting at the terminal to answer prompts, approve actions, or continue a conversation, so the invocation should use -p or --print to process a prompt and exit. Configuration files such as CLAUDE.md and project slash commands are still useful in this workflow because they give CI-invoked Claude Code the same standards, review criteria, and reusable instructions as the rest of the team. They solve what Claude should know or do, not how the CLI process should run. Plan mode is similarly a workflow choice for human review of complex changes, not the mechanism that prevents an unattended runner from hanging. For CI design, keep the mental model simple: use -p for unattended execution, add structured output options when downstream systems need machine-readable results, and keep project context in version-controlled configuration. Learn more in the Claude Code CLI reference.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. This team is adding SDK-managed subagents for code review and documentation work. They want Claude to route work to the right subagent based on its purpose, and they want the documentation subagent to read files but not edit or run commands. Which configuration should they use?

choices.text: Define a programmatic agents map keyed by subagent type, set each description and prompt, and give the documentation subagent a read-only tools allowlist.
Create subagent files with prompts only, use filenames as routing descriptions, and rely on parent permissions for tool limits.
Define agents by display name, put the subagent type inside prompt, and block editing tools through top-level disallowedTools.
Define top-level allowedTools for read-only tools, add routing guidance to CLAUDE.md, and omit per-subagent tool settings.

explanations.A: This uses the documented AgentDefinition pattern for SDK applications. The map key is the subagent type, description guides routing, prompt defines the subagent behavior, and tools restricts that subagent to only the listed tools.
explanations.B: Filesystem-based subagents are an alternative, but the question asks for SDK-managed subagents and routing based on purpose. For AgentDefinition objects, description and prompt are required, and omitting tools makes the subagent inherit all available parent tools.
explanations.C: The agents map key is the subagent type Claude invokes through the Agent tool, not just a display label. Top-level disallowedTools can block tools broadly, but it is not the same as configuring one subagent's allowed tool set with AgentDefinition.tools.
explanations.D: Top-level allowedTools auto-approves tools, but it is not a per-subagent restriction mechanism. CLAUDE.md can provide project context, but it does not replace AgentDefinition.description and AgentDefinition.prompt for SDK subagent definitions.

questions.questionExplanation: For SDK-managed subagents, the central configuration object is the AgentDefinition inside the programmatic agents option. Each entry is keyed by the subagent type, and that key is what Claude uses when invoking the Agent tool with subagent_type. The required description is the natural-language routing cue, while the required prompt acts as the subagent's system prompt. The important tool-control distinction is that AgentDefinition.tools is a subagent-specific allowlist. If it is omitted, the subagent inherits all tools available from the parent, which is not appropriate when a documentation subagent should be read-only. By contrast, top-level allowedTools or allowed_tools auto-approves tools, but does not restrict Claude to only those tools. Programmatic subagents are the recommended approach for SDK applications, and filesystem-based agents are a separate alternative. For more detail, see Anthropic's Agent SDK subagents guide and the Agent SDK TypeScript reference.

questions.question: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution. A custom /parallel-review command starts an SDK run in a repository pinned to a pre-v2.1.63 Claude Code configuration where subagent delegation is performed with `Task`. It should fan out across specialized review subagents. The current SDK options auto-approve only Read, Grep, and Glob, and each run pauses at the first attempted subagent delegation with an interactive permission prompt. What should the team change?

choices.text: Add `Task` to the coordinator SDK run's `allowedTools` or `allowed_tools` list.
Remove delegation tools from `allowedTools` and rely on permission prompts.
Add `Task` delegation guidance to `CLAUDE.md` for the project repository.
Add `Agent` only to worker subagents' `tools` lists for nested calls.

explanations.A: In this legacy configuration, subagent delegation is performed with `Task`, so the coordinator's SDK run must auto-approve that tool to avoid the permission prompt. Adding it to `allowedTools` or `allowed_tools` addresses the described pause during the first attempted delegation.
explanations.B: Removing the relevant delegation tool from `allowedTools` would not make unattended delegation smoother. The permission documentation states that listed tools are auto-approved, while unlisted tools fall through to permission handling unless separately blocked or denied.
explanations.C: `CLAUDE.md` provides project instructions and context, but it does not configure SDK tool permission approvals. Guidance may influence behavior, but it will not auto-approve the tool that is triggering the permission prompt.
explanations.D: A subagent's own `tools` list controls what that subagent can use, including whether it can spawn further subagents in current configurations. It does not auto-approve the parent coordinator's first delegation, which is where the described run is pausing.

questions.questionExplanation: For the legacy configuration described in the stem, subagent delegation is performed through Task, so the coordinator SDK run needs that delegation tool in allowedTools or allowed_tools. The practical issue is not that the subagents are undefined, it is that the first delegation attempt is not auto-approved and therefore falls into interactive permission handling. Current Claude Code documentation describes the renamed Agent tool for spawning subagents, and notes that Task was renamed to Agent in Claude Code v2.1.63. That version distinction matters: current configurations should generally use Agent, while a pinned legacy configuration that delegates with Task must auto-approve Task. Also remember that allowedTools is not a hard allowlist by itself. It auto-approves listed tools, while unlisted tools can still fall through to permission mode or a permission callback unless separately denied or locked down. See Sub-agents, Agent SDK subagents, and Agent SDK permissions.

questions.question: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives. The repository's main instruction file has grown to more than 400 lines and mixes review tone, test conventions, API design rules, and deployment checklist guidance. CI runs show that Claude Code is applying deployment guidance to routine unit test reviews and sometimes missing the test-specific criteria developers care about. What change should this team make to reduce irrelevant context while keeping shared review standards available?

choices.text: Move topic-specific guidance into Markdown files under .claude/rules/ and add paths frontmatter for rules that apply only to matching files.
Split the large instruction file into imported Markdown files and reference each one from the root CLAUDE.md with @path imports.
Move all topic guidance into .claude/rules/ files without paths frontmatter and rely on the directory to lazy-load them.
Create separate CLAUDE.md files in every package directory and duplicate the relevant test, API, and deployment guidance there.

questions.questionExplanation: A 400-line instruction file mixing four unrelated topics is exactly the case the docs address: "target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence. If your instructions are growing large, use path-scoped rules so instructions load only when Claude works with matching files." Splitting topics into `.claude/rules/` files and adding `paths` frontmatter to the ones that are file-specific keeps shared review standards loaded while deployment guidance stops bleeding into unit-test reviews. B is wrong because the docs state imported files "still load and enter the context window at launch," so `@path` imports improve organization but do not reduce irrelevant context. C is wrong because "rules without a `paths` field are loaded unconditionally and apply to all files" and are loaded at launch, so omitting frontmatter reproduces the current problem; the rules directory does not lazy-load by itself. D is wrong because duplicating guidance into per-package CLAUDE.md files creates drift and still loads unrelated topics wherever Claude reads files in those directories. Reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory

questions.question: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports. While maintaining the system described above, this team keeps citation validation tests beside the agent code they exercise, including files under packages/search/, packages/synthesis/, and apps/reporting/. The team wants Claude Code to apply the same testing conventions whenever editing these test files, without loading those conventions for unrelated production files. What should the team do?

choices.text: Add the testing conventions to the root CLAUDE.md so Claude Code always loads them for the repository.
Create separate CLAUDE.md files in each package directory that repeat the same testing conventions for local files.
Create a Markdown rule file under .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter using paths glob patterns for the test file names.
Add the testing conventions to each developer's user-level CLAUDE.md so Claude Code loads them during edits.

explanations.A: Root project memory is appropriate for universal project context, but these conventions are only relevant when editing test files. Loading them for all production code edits adds irrelevant context and does not use the path-specific rule capability.
explanations.B: Directory-level memory can add local context, but it is directory-bound rather than file-type-bound across the whole repository. Repeating the same convention in many directories is harder to maintain and can drift as packages are added or reorganized.
explanations.C: This uses Claude Code's path-specific rule mechanism for project instructions that should apply only to matching files. Glob patterns such as test file name patterns can match files by type across multiple directories, so the rule is not tied to a single folder layout.
explanations.D: User-level memory is a real Claude Code mechanism, but it is personal rather than shared through the project repository. It also applies too broadly, so test-only conventions can appear in contexts where the team wanted them excluded.

questions.questionExplanation: For conventions that should follow a file type rather than a directory, Claude Code path-specific rules are the right fit. A Markdown file in .claude/rules/ can include YAML frontmatter with the exact paths field, for example patterns that match test files wherever they live in the repository. This design avoids the maintenance burden of copying instructions into multiple directory-level CLAUDE.md files. It also avoids the context bloat of placing test-only guidance in a broadly loaded CLAUDE.md, whether at the project level or in each developer's user-level memory. The mental model is that CLAUDE.md is best for broadly applicable memory, while .claude/rules/ lets a project attach narrower instructions to matching paths. The rule files remain ordinary Markdown project files, and the documented paths frontmatter provides the conditional activation behavior. See Claude Code memory for the documented rule-file structure and path scoping.

questions.question: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate. A refund operation sometimes fails because the order is outside the return window, but the agent treats the MCP response as a successful refund and tells the customer it was completed. What change should this team make to communicate the tool failure correctly?

choices.text: Return a CallToolResult with `isError: true` and include structured failure details in the result content.
Return a CallToolResult with `isError: false` and include structured failure details in the result content.
Return a normal tool result containing an `error` field and ask the agent to infer failure from the content.
Raise a protocol-level server exception and include structured failure details in the exception message.

explanations.A: This uses the MCP tool error pattern directly. The camelCase `isError` flag on `CallToolResult` tells the MCP client and agent that the tool call itself completed but produced an application-level failure.
explanations.B: Setting `isError` to false communicates that the tool result is not an error. Even if the content describes a return-window failure, the explicit MCP flag would mark the result as successful.
explanations.C: Embedding an error object inside a successful result relies on the model interpreting content correctly. The MCP pattern provides an explicit failure signal through `isError`, which is more reliable than asking the agent to infer status from arbitrary fields.
explanations.D: Protocol-level errors are not the right mechanism for ordinary business failures from a valid tool invocation. A return-window violation should be communicated as a tool result error so the agent can decide whether to explain, retry, or escalate.

questions.questionExplanation: In MCP, a tool can be invoked successfully at the protocol level while still failing at the application or business-logic level. The right pattern is to return a CallToolResult that marks the result with isError: true, then put useful recovery context in the result content.
